text:
If you're starting over after a divorce and have no idea where you actually stand with money, start here. You don't need a budget or a fancy spreadsheet. You need three numbers: what comes in each month, what goes out, and how many months you could keep going if nothing changed. That's it. I made a free one-page sheet for exactly this, and it's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

Nobody tells you that the hardest part of starting over isn't the paperwork. It's opening your bank app and not knowing what you're about to see. Do it anyway, just once. Write down what came in last month and what went out, with no judging and no fixing. That's your starting point, and it's more useful than it feels. The free Starter Sheet at the link in bio gives you a place to write it.

Day one counts.

Whether you're newly divorced or years into rebuilding, here's the question I'd start with: how many months could you keep going if nothing changed? Not how much you have, but how many months it covers. It turns a scary pile of numbers into one thing you can actually work on. There's a free one-page sheet to figure it out, and it's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

Boring Money Monday, for anyone rebuilding their life. Money stops feeling like a monster when you can say three things out loud: what comes in, what goes out, and how long you could keep going. If you can't say them yet, that's okay, because most people can't when they're starting over. The free Three Numbers Starter Sheet walks you through it, and it's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

When you're starting over, everyone tells you what to cut. Nobody asks what you want to keep. So I'll ask: what's one thing in your life, even a small one, that you're not giving up while you rebuild? A coffee with a friend, a gym class, the good shampoo. It counts. Protect what's worth it first, then look at everything else. What's on your list?

Day one counts.

A hard truth about rebuilding after a divorce: a plan with no room for joy tends to fall apart. So decide on purpose what stays, even if it's small. A weekly walk, a favorite takeout night, a class you love. That's not being irresponsible, it's making a plan you can actually live in. What are you keeping?

Day one counts.

Here's a ten-minute exercise for anyone starting over. Write down five things you spend money on that you'd be sad to lose, then circle the two that matter most. Those go on your keep list, and you don't have to defend them to anyone. Everything else we can look at calmly, later. Which two did you circle?

Day one counts.

You're allowed to want a few nice things while you rebuild. Wanting them doesn't mean you're bad with money. It usually just means you're a person. Keep what makes your days feel like yours, then get honest about the rest. Follow along for one small money step a day, and tell me what's on your keep list.

Day one counts.

If money feels tight after a divorce, there are often a few quiet leaks you've never noticed. A subscription from two years ago, a free trial that turned into a charge, an app you forgot about. Scroll back one month in your bank app and circle anything you don't recognize or use. Part 2 of my $17 Day Zero Workbook, Where It Went, walks you through it step by step. It's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

Is there a phone call you've been dreading? Cancelling something, asking for a lower bill, calling a company that's still using your old name? I get it. The Dreaded Call Scripts in the Day Zero Workbook give you the words, so you can just read them out loud. The workbook is $17 and it's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

Autopay is wonderful until you forget what's on it. Set a timer for twenty minutes and list every bill that pulls money out automatically. You may find one to pause or cancel, and you'll probably feel a little more in control either way. The Year-at-a-Glance Bill Tracker in the $17 Day Zero Workbook gives you a place to keep it all. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

You don't have to slash everything to rebuild. You just have to look at it. In my method it goes Keep, Cut, Earn, Build, and cutting comes second on purpose, because you protect what's worth it first. The whole thing is in the 32-page Day Zero Workbook, $17, made for women starting over at any pace. It's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

Earning more while you're starting over doesn't have to mean a whole new career. Start smaller. Write down three things people already ask you for help with, maybe spreadsheets, writing, organizing, or fixing things. That list is where small ideas begin. No promises about money, just a place to look. What do people always ask you for help with?

Day one counts.

Here's something to think about this weekend. If all you had was a phone or a laptop, what could you do that someone would pay a fair price for? You don't need the whole answer, just one idea written down. Rebuilding is mostly small ideas that you finally put on paper. Drop yours below, and follow along for a small money step each day.

Day one counts.

Before you add any side income to your life, check what it will cost you in time. Five hours a week is five hours you have to find, and you're probably already tired. Look at your real calendar first. A small idea that fits your life beats a big one that doesn't. What would you say no to, to make room?

Day one counts.

You have more skills than your resume shows. Writing, organizing, teaching, fixing things, staying calm when everything's falling apart. Make a list of ten and don't edit it. Picking one to explore comes later. Today you're just reminding yourself what you bring to the table. What's the first skill on your list?

Day one counts.

Starting over feels easier with a first hour. List every account you have, write down every bill and when it's due, and change any password you reuse. None of it is glamorous, but it's the foundation everything else sits on. Part 4 of the $17 Day Zero Workbook, The First Hour, walks you through it. It's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

Some days you only have fifteen minutes and a little bit of hope. That's enough. The Fifteen-Minute Start is a bonus in the $17 Day Zero Workbook, for the days when you can only do one small thing. Small things add up when you keep showing up for them. It's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

Rebuilding your life after a divorce is slow, and that's fine. Fast and perfect isn't the goal. This week, one list of your accounts. Next week, one calendar of your bills. After that, one small cushion. The Day Zero Workbook, 32 pages for $17, lays out the order so you're not guessing. It's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

Before you sit down with a lawyer, an accountant, or a financial planner, it helps to know what to ask. Questions for a Money Helper is a bonus page in the $17 Day Zero Workbook. A licensed professional can help with the big decisions, and this helps you walk in prepared. It's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

If you're doing the money math at 2 A.M., you're not failing. You're scared, and that's allowed. Write the numbers down, close the notebook, and look again in daylight. They often look more manageable on paper than they do in your head. Who else has been up doing the 2 A.M. math? You're not the only one.

Day one counts.

When you start over, your brain asks why did I let this happen. Try swapping it for where did the money go. Why has no answer and it just hurts. Where is a question you can actually answer by opening one statement. Save this for the next time the why voice gets loud.

Day one counts.

topic: You don't have to feel ready
text:
You don't have to feel ready to start rebuilding. Nobody does. It's clumsy at first, and that's normal. Give yourself a slow week with one small task, and then rest. Zero isn't failing, zero is a starting line. Follow along and we'll keep the steps small together.

Day one counts.

A permission slip, for this weekend: you can go slowly. You can be bad at this at first. You can read the same page twice. You can start over at any age, from any place, divorced or not. Pick one tiny first move and only do that. Send this to a friend who needs to hear it.

Day one counts.

The Monthly Twenty is how I'd keep money feeling manageable: twenty calm minutes, once a month. Look at your three numbers, notice if anything changed, and pick one small step for the next month. That's the whole meeting. The free Three Numbers Starter Sheet is a good place to write them, and it's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

A Sunday reset, for anyone rebuilding: open your bank app, look at what came in and what went out this week, and write down one number you want to remember. Ten minutes, then close it. That's it. If you want somewhere to write it, the free Three Numbers Starter Sheet is at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

Once a month, I'd ask three questions. What came in? What went out? How many months could I keep going if nothing changed? If the answers moved, good, now you know. If they didn't, good, you're steady. Write them on one page with the free Three Numbers Starter Sheet, at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

Put the Monthly Twenty on your calendar like an appointment with a friend. Same day every month, same short list, no lecture. Looking at your money regularly is what makes it feel less scary over time. The free Three Numbers Starter Sheet makes it easy, and it's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.
